title: A Revolution That No Longer Needs Us

lines.text: Every technological revolution had a happy ending.
For one simple reason: machines still needed people.
That was the contract. It is about to expire.
In the eighteen-twenties, Britain had a quarter of a million handloom weavers.
The power loom bore them no malice. It was simply cheaper.
For half a century, output climbed, while wages stood still.
A generation lived out its life inside that chasm.
The happy ending came for their grandchildren, because railways needed stokers, signalmen, and clerks.
Only humans could fill those roles.
This time, that is precisely what has changed.
A loom only wove cloth. Today, one system writes code, drafts contracts, answers the phone, and tutors our children.
Screen work goes first. It is made of words, numbers and code.
Every revolution is a tug of war: displacement against reinstatement.
This time, the new jobs will belong to machines from birth.
Once a machine can do your job, its cost becomes the ceiling on your wage.
And that ceiling keeps falling. Below the rent. Below food. Below the cost of staying alive.
In nineteen-fifteen, America had twenty million horses. By nineteen-sixty, three million.
During the Irish Famine, a million people starved, while ships of grain sailed out of Irish ports.
In nineteen thirty-three, milk was poured onto highways and six million piglets were slaughtered, while cities went hungry.
The starving rarely lack food. They lack the ability to acquire it.
The abundance of machines will be priced, not shared.

card.title: When the Boat No Longer Needs the Water

lines.text: The ruler is the boat. The people are the water. The water can carry the boat, or capsize it.
A state that lives on oil answers only to those who hold the wells.
A.I. makes every economy a petrostate. Researchers call it the intelligence curse.
Our old weapons fail. A strike means nothing when no one needs your labor.
And an automated guard will never lower its weapon for a neighbor in the crowd.
We will sell what we own, piece by piece. The savings. The home. The business.
In fifteen-sixteen, Thomas More wrote that sheep were devouring men. Enclosure needed fences. This time, it needs only time.
Britain exported its unemployment: to India, to China, and across the ocean.
This time, there is no ocean left to cross. The machine arrives everywhere at once.
And the ladder's bottom rung, cheap labor, is the first thing it makes worthless.
The end will not arrive as an upheaval. It will come quietly.
The job posting never put up. The contract not renewed. The graduate who never finds a first job.
The weavers lost a craft. We are losing our place in the economy itself.
Our descendants will see the wealthiest, most dazzling world in history.
It will run flawlessly without them.
And not a single thing in it will belong to them.
